description: The wrist test measured your angle and your pain. If push-ups still hurt and the angle will not open, five mistakes are keeping the tunnels crowded. Here is the ninety-degree line, the traffic problem inside your wrist, and the errors that keep it loud for years.

beats.text: LEAN IN. READ ANGLE AND PAIN.

scenes.narration: Palms flat on the table again, fingers pointing back at you, elbows soft and straight. Lean your shoulders gently over your hands until the wrists reach their honest limit, and read both numbers this time: the ANGLE between forearm and the back of your hand, and the PAIN, zero to ten, that arrived with it. Then compare with your last test, if you have one. Is the angle opening? Is the pain retreating? Or are both numbers frozen while your push-ups still hurt and your planks still happen on fists? Frozen numbers in a wrist that gets used ten thousand times a day are never an anatomy problem alone. They are a management problem, and management problems have names. Five mistakes keep wrist tunnels crowded and loud for years, and at least one of them is considered good advice by almost everyone you know. Remember your angle and your pain. At the end, I match them to the mistakes.

scenes.label: THE LINE, READ BOTH WAYS
scenes.narration: The line is unchanged: NINETY degrees with a flat palm and no complaint is a wrist that can pay for any floor work you will ever do; sixty to ninety is the floor-work gap; pain before sixty is an irritated wrist. Today's second reading is motion between tests. Healing in this joint draws one specific graph: the angle climbing while the pain falls, the two numbers walking toward each other week by week. An angle climbing while pain climbs with it is not healing; it is forcing, and the wrist is keeping receipts. Pain falling while the angle never opens is half a recovery, a calm but permanently stiff joint. Frozen on both numbers, in a wrist being genuinely exercised, means the daily management around the exercise is re-crowding the tunnels as fast as the work clears them. That is where today's five mistakes live: not in your workout, in your week.
scenes.sub: 90 quiet: full toll - angle up pain up: forcing - frozen both: management

lines: in a tight tunnel complain loudly.
beats.title: THE CROWDING PROBLEM

scenes.narration: The wrist's problem is real estate. Every tendon that curls or opens your fingers, plus nerves and vessels, crosses this small joint through tight tunnels of tissue, with no spare room in the design. When the tendons are calm and slim, traffic flows and the joint is silent at any angle. When they are irritated and slightly swollen, the same tunnels become a crowded crossing where every movement is negotiated and extension, the push-up position, tightens the crossing most of all. This is why wrist pain feels so disproportionate to the size of the joint: it is not damage volume, it is traffic density. And it dictates the order of operations for everything in this episode. You cannot strengthen your way out of a traffic jam, and you cannot stretch a tunnel wider by force. First calm the traffic, then widen the road with graded load, then drive on it. Space is the therapy, and everything else is scheduling.

A word in defence of the workaround, because pride ruins more wrists than push-ups do. Training your pressing on fists or handles, wrist straight, while the angle is being rebuilt is not a lesser version of the exercise. It trains the chest, shoulders, triceps, and core at full value while billing the wrist nothing, which is exactly what a good bridge does: it keeps the rest of your life moving while one structure is under repair. The people who refuse the bridge face a false choice between grinding the wrist raw and stopping pressing entirely, and both options lose. Meanwhile the angle itself is rebuilt off to the side, in its own graded program: wall leans, counter leans, isometric presses, each step earned by quiet mornings. When the flat palm is finally paid for, you return to it with a stronger press than the day you left. That is not a detour. That is the road.

Now audit the hours, because the wrist signs its contract there. The modern wrist types in hovered flexion, scrolls with an overworked thumb, grips a wheel, a phone, a bar, and then twice a week is asked to slam into ninety degrees under bodyweight. Tissue keeps the ranges it visits and surrenders the rest, and extension is the least visited range in the modern hand's life. The renegotiation is mostly furniture and habits: a keyboard setup that lets the wrist float neutral instead of cocked, a mouse that fits the hand instead of pinching it, phone breaks, and small daily visits to the extended position at loads the wrist finds boring. None of this is the exercise program, and all of it decides whether the exercise program works. A wrist cannot be rehabbed for twenty minutes a day against twenty-three hours of contrary evidence. Change the evidence.

Your advantage is the width of the steps. Wrist progress is measured in centimetres of lean and degrees of angle, and your bodyweight makes each step small enough to stay inside the healing band. A heavy man's wall press is already a serious load for an irritated wrist; yours is a polite suggestion, adjustable by moving your feet a few centimetres. That granularity is the whole therapy for small structures with narrow tolerance bands: the dose must be tunable finer than the tissue's ability to complain. Your build is a fine instrument in a game that punishes blunt ones. The strong guys grind this joint because grinding is their only gear. You have gears they do not: wall, counter, fists, handles, floor, each one a legitimate station. Use all of them, in order, without embarrassment.
Now load it with me. Palm on the table, press down gentle and steady, no movement, no pain spike. Thirty seconds each side, fifteen to rest, three rounds. Go.

beats.text: 3. STRETCHING IT LIKE IT OWES YOU

scenes.narration: The five mistakes that keep wrists loud for years. One: grinding full push-ups through pain because the program demands it, re-crowding the tunnels daily. Two: refusing the fists, letting pride convert a bridge into a barrier and losing months of pressing. Three: stretching the wrist aggressively into its painful end range, trying to tear open a door that only opens for calm traffic. Four: the brace as a lifestyle, immobilising the joint into weakness and stiffness while calling it recovery. Five: ignoring the keyboard hours, perfect rehab performed inside a day that argues the opposite for ten hours. The thread through all five is order: calm the traffic, grade the load, renegotiate the hours, then drive. And the standing line of this season: wrist pain that began with a fall on an outstretched hand, swelling, clicking with weakness, numb fingers, or numbers frozen despite honest work, see a professional if it persists. Wrists hide fractures and ligament injuries well.

scenes.label: THEN WE LEAN IN AGAIN
scenes.narration: So, your grade. Pain before sixty degrees means calm first: isometrics and easy range, fists for all pressing, until the mornings quieten. Sixty to ninety is the floor-work gap: climb the staircase, wall to counter to floor, one station per few weeks, and let the two numbers walk toward each other. Ninety and quiet means the toll is paid in full and the floor is yours. Whatever your numbers, you leave today knowing the wrist's whole logic: it is a crowded crossing that heals in an order, calm, grade, drive, and it punishes anyone who reverses the order with months of noise. Put your angle in the comments. Just the number. We lean in again in thirty days.
scenes.sub: pain before 60: calm first - 60-90: the staircase - 90 quiet: full toll

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, same table, same gentle lean, and we grade that wrist again. Subscribe, because next the season turns: no more mistake files, just the wrong way and the right way, side by side. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
